title: Self-compassion test: how kind are you to yourself? Free quiz — cv.cm
description: Free self-compassion test: rate 14 statements about how you treat yourself when you fail, struggle or feel bad, and get a score from 0 to 56 with tips to be kinder to yourself. No sign-up; answers stay in your browser.
scoreLabel: Self-compassion score (0 = harsh on yourself, 56 = kind to yourself)
lede: When you mess up, are you your own worst critic or a steady friend? Rate 14 statements about how you treat yourself in hard moments to see how self-compassionate you are.
about: Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you'd treat a good friend who is having a hard time. The psychologist Kristin Neff describes three parts: kindness to yourself instead of harsh self-judgment, remembering that everyone struggles instead of feeling alone with it, and noticing painful feelings in a balanced way instead of drowning in them or pushing them away. Research links self-compassion with less anxiety and depression and more resilience, and it isn't the same as self-pity or letting yourself off the hook: self-compassionate people tend to own their mistakes and try again.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around those three parts. They are not Neff's Self-Compassion Scale or any other published questionnaire, and half of them describe being hard on yourself, so agreeing with everything lands in the middle. Your score is a starting point for reflection, not a measurement, and self-compassion is a skill you can build.

faq.a: Being kind and understanding toward yourself when you fail or suffer, remembering that struggling is part of being human, and holding painful feelings in awareness without exaggerating or ignoring them.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and the self-critical statements are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 moderate and 38 or more high.

faq.q: Is self-compassion the same as self-esteem?
faq.a: No. Self-esteem is how much you value yourself, often by comparing yourself with others. Self-compassion is how you treat yourself, and it doesn't depend on being better than anyone. The self-esteem check measures the other one.

faq.q: How can I be more self-compassionate?
faq.a: When you notice harsh self-talk, ask what you'd say to a friend in the same spot and say that to yourself. Put a hand on your chest, take a slow breath, and remind yourself that other people feel this too.

items: When I make a mistake, I talk to myself the way I'd talk to a good friend.
When I fail at something that matters, I call myself names in my head.
When things go wrong, I remember that everyone struggles sometimes.
When I'm struggling, it seems everyone else has life figured out.
When I feel bad, I can notice the feeling without getting swept away by it.
After something upsets me, I go over it again and again for days.
I accept my flaws as part of being human.
I'm harsh with myself about the parts of me I don't like.
When I'm going through a hard time, I give myself the care I need.
When I let myself down, I feel I don't deserve kindness.
When I fall short, I can feel disappointed without beating myself up.
When I notice something I dislike about myself, I feel set apart from other people.
I can see my problems in proportion, without making them bigger than they are.
When I'm hurting, I tell myself to just get over it.

low.name: Low self-compassion (0–18)
low.body: You're often hard on yourself: mistakes feel like proof that something is wrong with you, and hard times can feel lonely. That inner critic usually started as a way to push yourself, but it tends to wear you down rather than help. Try one small change: when you notice harsh self-talk, ask what you'd say to a friend and say that instead. If self-criticism comes with low mood that won't lift, talking to a counselor can help.

moderate.name: Moderate self-compassion (19–37)
moderate.body: You can be kind to yourself some of the time, but in harder moments the critic often takes over. That's where most people land. Notice which situations switch you into self-judgment, such as work, your body or relationships, and practice treating yourself there the way you would a friend. A slow breath and a reminder that everyone struggles go a long way.

high.name: High self-compassion (38–56)
high.body: You treat yourself with real kindness: you own your mistakes without tearing yourself apart, you remember you're not alone in struggling and you can hold hard feelings without being swallowed by them. That steadiness is linked with resilience and wellbeing. Keep it up, and share it: people around you can learn it from you.
